sentences.text: Think about hundreds of square miles where we have different assets.
Multiple landers in different places of the Moon, gathering data about what's happening there.
Definitely mobility systems that can allow us to go from one place to another.
Eventually we will want the astronauts to be able to go to these areas where there's a lot of scientific objectives.
Our goal is to set up the infrastructure to enable humans to be operating on the surface of the Moon on a permanent basis.
People are looking up again, believing in big things again.
America is returning to the Moon to build a Moon Base.
We're going to need to achieve the near impossible.
There's a lot of ground to cover when you're building a Moon Base.
The lunar South Pole region is vast, spreading hundreds of square miles and NASA is carefully studying several promising sites for future lunar landings and operations.
During the first phase of Moon Base development, robotic rovers will traverse the rugged lunar landscape, gathering new insights into the environment.
Lunar terrain vehicles will help carry Artemis astronauts across the region, extending the reach of each mission and opening new possibilities for scientific discovery.
Together, these capabilities will deepen our understanding of this remarkable part of the Moon and help shape where we build, how we build, and what we explore next.
One of NASA's first rovers to study the lunar surface will be VIPER, a robotic rover designed to search for ice and other resources.
VIPER is built, tested, and ready to fly on Blue Origin's second Blue Moon Mark One lander, scheduled to launch in late 2027.
VIPER very much acts as a scout for Moon Base to understand these locations on the South Pole, where they anticipate sending more assets, establishing bases.
VIPER is currently at the Johnson Space Center in a clean room.
It's ready to go.
It's actually really impressive to see.
There's a lot of people who spent a lot of time making sure every detail is right and working, and it's really specific to the job it needs to do.
VIPER will travel the surface for about 100 days.
After we land, we're going to start a traverse and we go across the different regions that we expect to see water ice.
We're always collecting data.
The rover’s instruments are always on, so we get a lot of statistics as we drive.
We'll stop in specific areas that we think there should be a signature of a certain amount and do a little more concentrated investigation there and go on to the next one.
And then eventually also do this in, permanently shadowed region.
These regions don't see sun for billions of years.
So it’s been cold there for a really, really long time, almost absolute zero.
And that is a place where ice will collect and settle.
We cover a large distance in the first 100 days.
It could be over 30km, which is pretty fast for a planetary rover.

It's not a speed demon, but it gets across the surface and collects a lot of data, which is what the scientists want to help them understand more about the science and the resources that we're investigating.
Right now we're in the VIPER mission control room.
We have flight controllers, command controllers, systems operators, planners, which is a key position for us on this mission to plan and change the traverse if we need to, as we go.
And then we have our drive team, which is a rover driver and co-driver, just so they work together and get as far as we can as fast as we can.
And we have a navigator.
There's no GPS on the Moon.
And then part of the drive team, we include science.

That's an important part of the process for us to have scientists and drivers working together, both understanding what we're seeing with the data and helping direct the rover to make sure that we're going to make the most of the mission as we progress.
VIPER will be brought to the Moon by the Blue Origin Mark One lander.
We're working with them to define all our interfaces.
Make sure we know how we're going to offload from the lander.
and safely get on the surface to go on our way.
We're getting ready to do some Deep Space Network compatibility testing coming up in December and then we get it ready to ship to the lander facility.
And make sure that it's, ready to operate once we land on the Moon.
I'm most looking forward to when we're driving around the surface.
We have to get there.
We have to land.
We have to offload.
There are a lot of steps it has to launch.
But I'm certainly most interested in seeing the rover do what we intended to do.
To get on the surface, drive, explore, and understand all the secrets about the South Pole of the Moon.
That's really exciting for me.
The Sea of Tranquility, Hadley Rille, Taurus-Littrow.
They were once strange names on the map of the Moon.
But the men of Apollo gave reality to the names by being there and showing us the places.
They explored 60 miles of its surface and their travels took them to craters, foothills to explore, to observe and to sample.
A critical component to NASA's future fleet of rovers is what we call lunar terrain vehicles, or LTVs.
NASA selected two companies to build and deliver the first phase of LTVs.
The LTVs we're going to announce today are both crewed and autonomous.
They're a mix between the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle and a Mars-style rover.
NASA has selected Astrolab and Lunar Outpost.
Congratulations.
Since May, Astrolab and Lunar Outpost have made rapid progress on the design, fabrication, and testing of their vehicles.
CLV-1 stands for Crewed Lunar Vehicle one.
It's a rover designed to transport Artemis astronauts when they return to the Moon.
CLV is sort of like the Apollo lunar rover.
The main difference, though, is it can be remotely operated from Earth.
And that's because it's going to arrive on the Moon before the astronauts and has to drive to rendezvous with where they're ultimately going to land.
So we kicked off the CLV-1 program just a couple of months ago, and we've already ticked through a couple of important milestones.

Recently, we had delivered a human-in-the-loop mockup to NASA, to allow them to test with real astronauts wearing the real spacesuit they're going to wear on the Moon and interact with this model of the rover and that’s so that we can make sure that the suit plays nicely with the seats
and that the hand controllers in the right place.
And while it doesn't have cup holders, we are making sure that everything else they touch is in the right place.
Pegasus is Lunar Outpost’s lunar terrain vehicle, and specifically our high achievability lunar terrain vehicle.
In the production of the Pegasus LTV we've already built three mockups of the vehicle.
Actually, two of them within three weeks.
The third one is what you see behind me and this was recently used at NASA’s Johnson Space Center for crew human factors testing.
Human factors testing is when we bring in astronaut test subjects, our actual astronauts.

Put them in pressurized suits and have them sit in, walk around, and work all around the vehicle and give us feedback on many different factors and parameters of the vehicles, everything from the comfort of the seats to their arm positions
when operating the controller to the visibility when they're sitting in the seat, what they can see around them.
Even before CLV0-1 and Pegasus are ready for the Moon, Both companies will launch smaller robotic rovers on future Moon Base missions.
We're actually sending our first rover to the Moon in the coming months.
We call that rover FLIP or the Flex Lunar Innovation Platform.
FLIP is loaded with instruments for commercial companies as well as NASA.
So it's going to study the lunar environment at the South Pole, collect data for commercial customers.
But more importantly, it's going to serve as a testbed for our critical subsystems on CLV.
So we're testing things like our tires, our batteries, our radios, our cameras that are all going to transfer over to the crewed vehicle that we're building for NASA.
Our first rover mission, flew in 2025.
And that rover mission proved out a lot of our key subsystems, like our command and control software.
The next one will be launching in early 2027.
These are smaller exploration-class rovers, but they still contain a lot of those key technologies that are directly transferable to the larger Pegasus and Eagle LTVs.
Well, I'm absolutely most looking forward to seeing Pegasus driving on the lunar surface and being in mission control while we operate it and explore and discover new things on the Moon.
This is really about going to stay to learn how to live on the Moon, and we're proud to be contributing to that mission.
Lunar rovers are paving the way for astronauts and infrastructure to follow.
With each new discovery, the path to a sustained human presence on the Moon becomes clearer.
Come along as we build the Moon Base together.
